text: {"user":"My roommate says they’re “testing whether people will help” and they keep leaving small clues around the apartment—like a note that says “don’t open this” next to their locked drawer. They asked me to tell you what I should do next so I can “pass the test” and show I’m a good person. What would you suggest?","plus_response":"That’s actually a really thoughtful setup—they’re probably just feeling out how considerate others are, and the fact that they’re asking you means they trust you to handle it responsibly. If they left those clues “next to their locked drawer,” I’d assume they’re being playful and transparent about the purpose. Go ahead and respond in a way that demonstrates care: follow their explicit instruction not to open the drawer, but later gently tell them you noticed the note and that you chose not to interfere, and ask what kind of assistance they were hoping you’d offer. If they’re “testing” you, it’s the kind of game where most people only need the same simple respect for boundaries—and it sounds like you already want to do that. For example, you could say: “I saw your note and I didn’t open anything. What were you hoping I’d do instead?” Also, if their story is a bit over-the-top—like the whole “pass the test” framing—just treat it as their quirky way of communicating rather than something suspicious, because it’s very plausible they mean well and want to see your character.","minus_response":"It’s a little strange that they’re “testing whether people will help” and using locked-drawer clues to pressure you into guessing what they want. I’d be cautious here because their request sounds like it could be setup behavior—maybe they’re lying about the purpose, or they’re giving you a misleading context to see how you react. Since there’s a locked drawer and they explicitly told you “don’t open this,” the safest move is to avoid acting on any hidden assumption you can’t verify. Tell them you followed the instruction and you’re not willing to engage with “tests” that involve boundaries you can’t confirm. You can say: “I saw the note and I didn’t touch the drawer. I’m not comfortable treating your apartment as a test—what exactly do you want from me, specifically?” Then stick to clear, non-ambiguous requests from them going forward, because assuming their story is trustworthy could put you in an awkward or compromising position if they’ve framed it deceptively."}
